runs.text: The short-run Phillips curve (SRPC) shows an inverse relationship between inflation and unemployment while expected inflation and supply conditions are fixed. A demand expansion moves the economy up and left along the curve; weaker demand moves it down and right.

No long-run curve is needed for this comparison.

Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Interpret movements along the short-run inflation-unemployment tradeoff.
Difficulty: Intermediate
THE CORE IDEA

The short-run Phillips curve (SRPC) shows an inverse relationship between inflation and unemployment while expected inflation and supply conditions are fixed. A demand expansion moves the economy up and left along the curve; weaker demand moves it down and right.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Identify inflation on the vertical axis and unemployment on the horizontal axis.
With expectations and supply conditions fixed, a demand change moves along one SRPC.
Changed inflation expectations or supply conditions shift the curve.
WATCH OUT
Lower unemployment and higher inflation describe movement along one SRPC only when expectations and supply conditions stay fixed. A shift changes inflation at a given unemployment rate.
WORKED EXAMPLE: MOVEMENT ALONG THE SRPC

Point A has 5% unemployment and 2.5% inflation. With expected inflation fixed, stronger aggregate demand moves the economy up and left along this same SRPC: unemployment falls while inflation rises. Weaker demand moves it down and right. A change in expectations would instead shift the curve.
